topStories.headline: New Vendor Law Shows Early Results on Mission Street, But Nighttime Challenges Persist
topStories.dek: Nearly 400 warnings and 52 citations issued in first two months under California's SB 276, which targets suspected stolen goods sold without permits.
topStories.body:
Two months after San Francisco began enforcing SB 276 — a law authored by state Senator Scott Wiener and co-sponsored by Mayor Daniel Lurie specifically for San Francisco — the Mission District's commercial corridors are showing signs of improvement, according to vendors, police, and business owners. The law authorizes SFPD to cite people selling commonly stolen goods without a permit or proof of purchase, addressing a gap created by a 2018 state law that decriminalized sidewalk vending.

According to city data, police have issued 396 warnings, 46 first-time citations, and six second-time citations. No misdemeanor arrests have been made. SFPD Officer Robert Rueca described the department's approach as education-first: "It's really about teaching these violators that there's better ways to conduct business," he told ABC7.

Rodrigo Lopez, president of the Mission Street Vendors Association, said the city has made significant progress. He noted that the neighborhood's 33 permitted vendors are now operating in designated locations between 22nd and 25th streets, and he supports enforcement targeting unpermitted sellers. "The city has control over that issue," Lopez said.

Officials acknowledge that enforcement challenges remain, particularly during overnight hours due to staffing limitations. The Board of Supervisors approved a list of more than 100 commonly stolen items subject to the new rules when the law took effect last December. SB 276 applies strictly to non-food merchandise; street food vendors operate under a separate ordinance, SB 395, which the Board approved in March over objections from vendors who said its commissary kitchen requirements are too costly.

topStories.headline: ICE Electronic Monitoring of Immigrants Expands Across San Francisco Area, Including Mission
topStories.dek: New Mission Local reporting reveals thousands of Bay Area immigrants — many without criminal records — are tethered to ankle monitors, smartphone apps, and wrist devices under the federal ISAP program.
topStories.body:
A new investigation by Mission Local published August 5 documents the growing use of electronic monitoring devices on immigrants in the San Francisco area, including Mission District residents. According to a July data release by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 16,765 people in the program use the SmartLINK smartphone app, 3,624 wear ankle monitors, and 415 wear wrist-worn devices.

Immigration attorneys cited in the report say they are observing a significant increase — both in the frequency of electronic monitoring and the duration that immigrants are required to wear the devices — under the Trump administration's approach to the ICE Alternatives to Detention (ISAP) program. The devices intensively track location and can complicate work and daily life.

The story follows a pattern documented by national reporters: a June 2025 internal ICE memo directed officers to equip noncitizens in the program with GPS monitors "whenever possible," and the number of people wearing ankle monitors nearly tripled in the months that followed. Immigration advocates in the Mission have been organizing support for affected families, and legal aid organizations have flagged concerns about the lack of individualized assessment before devices are assigned.

topStories.headline: Former Mission KFC-Taco Bell to Become Affordable Community Recording Studio
topStories.dek: San Francisco musician Jeremy Rosenblum has purchased the long-vacant fast-food building at Duboce and Guerrero to transform it into an accessible hub for independent artists.
topStories.body:
A shuttered KFC-Taco Bell at the corner of Duboce Avenue and Guerrero Street in the Mission District is being reimagined as an affordable recording studio and creative space for local musicians, CBS San Francisco reported in May. Musician and independent recording engineer Jeremy Rosenblum purchased the long-vacant property with plans to serve artists who lack access to professional equipment.

Rosenblum told KPIX that his intention is to help people who would not otherwise be able to go into a first-class studio record and distribute their music. He described the building as an "iconic piece" of the neighborhood that residents recognized immediately. The project draws on Rosenblum's experience running Studio SQ, an affordable studio he operated in Bayview from 2003 to 2013.

According to KRON4, construction was expected to begin in June 2026 once a final building permit was approved, with the full renovation estimated to take 18 months to two years. When complete, the space aims to provide a community music hub at a location long familiar to Mission residents — bringing new creative energy to a corridor that has seen years of commercial vacancy.

moreNews.headline: CMC Garden Volunteer Day Kicks Off New Quarter at Mission District Music School
moreNews.body: The San Francisco Community Music Center at 544 Capp Street in the Mission District is inviting community volunteers to a summer gardening session on Saturday, August 8, from 8 AM to noon. Volunteers are asked to bring shears and gloves for a community beautification effort in the Mozart Garden and Courtyard ahead of the new fall quarter. Coffee and donuts provided. The CMC, founded in 1921, serves over 3,100 students annually from its Mission District branch.

moreNews.headline: Bernal Heights Village Marketplace Returns Three More Saturdays in August
moreNews.body: The Bernal Village Marketplace, which transforms a historic 1924 former Bank of America building at 433 Cortland Avenue into a curated indoor pop-up market, is scheduled for three consecutive Saturdays in August: the 16th, 23rd, and 30th, from 11 AM to 5 PM. The marketplace features 10–12 rotating vendors offering handmade goods at accessible price points — vendor fees run $40–$50, far below the $100–$500+ charged at many other SF markets — making it a launchpad for emerging local entrepreneurs. Free admission.

moreNews.headline: Precita Eyes Mural Tours Continue Every Weekend Through Summer
moreNews.body: Precita Eyes Muralists, the nonprofit founded in 1977 at 2981 24th Street in the Mission District, continues to offer weekend guided mural walks led by muralists through the end of summer. Tours cover Balmy Alley and the wider Mission District, exploring murals both historic and newly painted. Tickets are available at the door on Saturday mornings starting at 11 AM: $25 general admission, $15 seniors, $10 youth. Private and group tours are also available by appointment any day of the week.
